RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Alemans in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Black Forest & Main Valley, merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Alemans was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Black Forest & Main Valley, cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Auxiliaries along the Main Valley road shovel frozen ruts out of the wheel tracks while supply wagons creak past. Their cured meat has gone green, and the watch officer counts the copper coins left in each tent before roll call. Helmet linings are patched with wool scraps, and a spearman who loses his mail shirt in a river crossing will serve the rest of the campaign in a leather jerkin.

Word from the Black Forest ironworks says the levy for the autumn campaign is delayed by two weeks. A lord who wants his knights mounted must sell surplus timber to merchants bound for the river markets, and must do it quietly, because rival barons watch every cart that leaves the gate.
